extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in recommender systems, NLP/ML for news recommendation, and news-technology designers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for designing, implementing, and assessing news recommender systems (NRS), covering timeliness, user modeling, content-quality control, deep-learning models, evaluation metrics, and societal effects/mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / recency-based ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: An article’s likelihood of being chosen is proportional to its current popularity (count). News stories can also be ranked according to their popularity in popular micro-blogging sites like Twitter; trends are also used to determine popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity-based and timeliness models are easy to implement, but do not ensure credibility — false news may be more popular and more likely to be retweeted. Traditional timeliness models may be limited in addressing dynamic user behaviors in an NRS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity-based ranking (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ranking by popularity (counts, retweets, trending) to surface news items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While straightforward, popularity ranking can surface non-credible or false stories (e.g., false stories that are more likely to be retweeted). Popularity must be tempered with credibility and other quality measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: User modeling: explicit vs implicit feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Users’ preferences are modeled via explicit feedback (quantifiable ratings) and implicit feedback (clicks, browsing history, reading time, percentage scrolled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit feedback is used when users do not provide explicit ratings; examples include clicks, reading-time, and scroll percentage (5%, 50%, 75%). Models should account for both modalities and their noisiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: User modeling: anonymous and registered profiling considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: NRS must consider anonymous readers, profile information for registered users, passive consumption, negative implicit feedbacks, and relevance of readers’ intents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs must address varying availability of profile data (anonymous vs registered) and model passive/negative signals and intent to improve personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypical user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a user to a stereotype class inferred from co-occurring characteristics (e.g., geolocation, user habits) and infer preferences from class priors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when background knowledge is incomplete. Known issues: cannot learn completely new stereotypes; excessive stereotyping may produce segregated groups or filter bubbles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-based user/article modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent news articles via content features (categories, headlines, sources, topics) using BoW, TF-IDF, Hashing, Word2Vec, etc., and recommend items similar to user-read content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional statistical methods are limited because they often ignore semantics and context and struggle to capture time-ordered dependencies and volatile/anonymous user preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative filtering (CF) user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Model based on users’ interactions; collect interests from similar users and use histories to recommend without analyzing item features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CF does not require item feature analysis but needs temporal distinctions preserved — lack of temporal sequencing can impair predicting the next article. Incorporate time-sequence information or session-based methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-based user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply semantics, ontologies (e.g., IPTC), or knowledge bases (Wikipedia, Microsoft Satori) to build rich content profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows reuse of domain knowledge and richer semantics, but building/updating knowledge bases and ontologies can be expensive and present scalability/multilingual challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microblogging-based user modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer user interest profiles from social media (microblogs like Twitter) and use them to provide personalized and trending news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microblogs provide rich interaction data but require quality assessment — microblog content can be less trustworthy than curated news and needs additional filtering/measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite / temporal user modeling requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: User modeling in NRS should include users’ histories and also short-term, seasonal, diversified, and sequential interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because news preferences are volatile and many users are anonymous, composite models that capture multiple temporal scales and diversity of interests are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content quality control (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality control for news content addresses handling massive unstructured textual data in real time and evaluating content quality beyond efficiency/scalability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key issues in content quality include duplication, lack of semantics, spamming (clickbait), and biases. Qualitative (gold-standard/human) and quantitative analyses are both used; qualitative is time-consuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and remove duplicate/similar content that appears across multiple URLs and publishers to avoid repeated recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional methods use TF-IDF/BoW, thresholds on similarity, clustering (k-means) and selecting representatives. Limitations: scaling to large corpora and generating embeddings for many articles; simple content-similarity may miss paraphrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantics-based content representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture semantics from news structure metadata (taxonomy), ontologies, or concepts/named entities (e.g., via Wikipedia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-level semantics from metadata/ontologies can improve representation but may fall short of full coverage (news body, titles). Challenges include changing ontologies, scalability, and multilingualism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias detection in news content
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect bias in news articles (publisher, author, style, tone) using methods like sentiment analysis and exploration–exploitation strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiment-bearing word detection and exploration–exploitation can indicate bias levels, but these methods are limited and more research is needed to measure and mitigate evolving bias tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clickbait detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify deceptive/clickbait headlines from regular headlines using classifiers trained on labeled clickbait datasets drawn from domains known for clickbait (BuzzFeed, Upworthy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers rely on linguistic and syntactic cues; however, tactics change over time (concept drift), so models require periodic retraining and inclusion of new semantics/patterns to remain effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep learning: representation learning for multimodal news
rubrics_metrics.description: DL models (CNNs/RNNs/BERT) learn representations from multimodal data (text, images, audio, video) and avoid manual feature engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DL is strong at handling large multimodal content and creating embeddings useful for downstream recommendation tasks; choose architectures appropriate to modality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep learning: modeling complex user-item interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: DL models can learn multiple, rich interactions between users and items beyond linear MF approaches (e.g., via MLPs, attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neural approaches (e.g., NCF) show performance gains over traditional CF by modeling non-linear user-item relations; use when interaction complexity warrants it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep learning: sequential modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: DL methods (RNNs, Transformers) are effective at modeling temporal dynamics and session-based recommendation tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential models capture user behavior over time better than static CF/CBF; session creation should preserve chronological item clicks/publication times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep learning: cold-start and data sparsity mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: DL can extract features from news and user data to improve estimation of profiles when explicit rating information is sparse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation learning from content and side-information helps alleviate cold-start issues for users/items without much interaction history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation emphasis on accuracy and need for beyond-accuracy metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Current NRS research (including DL-based) tends to focus on accuracy and offline evaluation protocols; aspects beyond accuracy — novelty, serendipity, diversity, composite user model — are underexplored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should measure and balance beyond-accuracy metrics (novelty, serendipity, diversity) alongside accuracy; offline protocols dominate but may miss real-world effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-layer perceptron (MLP) as neural MF extension
rubrics_metrics.description: MLP is a feed-forward neural network used to add non-linear transformations on top of matrix factorization to learn rich user-item interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MLP-based architectures (e.g., NCF) are simple and efficient for extending MF; use to capture non-linearities in interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autoencoders (AE) for representation learning
rubrics_metrics.description: AEs learn to reconstruct inputs via an encoder–decoder and are used to learn low-dimensional representations of users/items and compress sparse rating matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denoising and stacked AEs can create robust article representations and extract low-dimensional features from sparse data for recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) for local text features
rubrics_metrics.description: CNNs apply convolution and pooling to extract local features (e.g., n-gram-like) from headlines or full news bodies and perform faster with fewer parameters than MLP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNNs are useful for text and multimodal feature extraction and reduce manual feature engineering; often used for headline/body representation then similarity-based recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrent neural networks (RNN) for sequence modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: RNNs (LSTM, GRU) model variable-length sequences and are used for session-based and sequence-aware recommendation; GRU is faster, LSTM better for longer sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants include unidirectional vs bidirectional LSTM, and RNNs augmented with neural attention to capture richer sequential features. Choice depends on sequence length and computational constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural attention mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention allows a model to focus on informative parts of input; used at word-level and news-level to weigh words or news pieces differently (e.g., headlines vs body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalized attention uses user embeddings as query vectors so informativeness differs per user. Attention helps filter noise and underpins Transformers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph neural networks (GNN) for reader-news-topic graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: GNNs operate on graph structures (nodes, edges) and can be applied to reader-news-topic graphs to learn embeddings for classification/prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GNNs perform well when combined with attention; use when relations between readers, news, and topics form useful graph structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformer models / self-attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformers use self-attention to process sequences in parallel and have been successful in NLP; pre-trained models (BERT, BART, GPT, RoBERTa) transfer knowledge to downstream tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformers (and pretrained language models like BERT) have been applied to model user behavior sequences and news representations; applicable when large pretraining resources or transfer learning are feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement learning (RL) for sequential decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: RL (e.g., DQN) frames recommendation as trial-and-error with agents, environments, states, actions, and rewards to learn sequences of decisions maximizing expected future rewards (clicks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RL can model dynamics in user preferences and optimize long-term reward sequences; consider design of reward functions and sample efficiency in online/offline settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-algorithmic effects on readers' behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms can have societal/behavioral effects such as filter bubble, echo chamber, polarization, fragmentation of public sphere, dehumanization, biased assimilation, denial to counter-attitudinal behavior, reinforced digital gate-keeping, and enabling deep fakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRS designers should be aware of these risks and evaluate systems not only on accuracy but on their potential to produce these negative outcomes; interdisciplinary work (journalism, political science) is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective exposure as design consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective exposure (people preferring information aligned with their views) affects consumption; NRS should consider it when designing for diverse exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is mixed: some studies show people seek pro-attitudinal content while others show exposure to counter-attitudinal information via social networks. Incorporate design elements that encourage balanced exposure where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity-aware algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms that incorporate diversity at re-ranking or optimization phases to promote exposure to unpopular/long-tail items and diverse topics, styles, tags, perspectives, and ideologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity can be included during re-ranking or baked into optimization (multi-objective). Examples: taxonomy expansion, exploration–exploitation bandits, regularization approaches. Balance diversity with accuracy to retain personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudge theory (ethical nudging) in UI/algorithm design
rubrics_metrics.description: Small design changes (nudges) can encourage users toward broader or more balanced news consumption; nudges can be used transparently and ethically to influence choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nudges have been misused (steering toward sensational/fake content). Implement transparent, ethically-designed nudges (browser add-ons, interface cues) to encourage desirable behaviors without excessive monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs among evaluation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist quantifiable trade-offs between metrics (accuracy-coverage, accuracy-diversity, accuracy-serendipity, diversity-serendipity), and combining accuracy with beyond-accuracy measures can improve user behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate algorithms on multiple metrics and quantify trade-offs; techniques include multi-objective optimization, bandits, and regularization to balance competing objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect-level diversification (aspects as diversification attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect is a collection of attributes/components used to categorize information (topics, styles, tags, sentiments) and can be used to diversify recommendations by presenting different perspectives on a news topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify/cluster news by aspects and present aspect-level perspectives to users; aspect-level presentation is underexplored but promising for balanced exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration–exploitation strategies (bandits) for balancing accuracy and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multi-arm bandit methods with exploration–exploitation optimization to trade off immediate accuracy with diversity/exposure goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bandits can promote long-tail items and discover user preferences; tune exploration schedules and reward definitions to balance objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularization techniques to encode diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate diversity via regularization (e.g., Ridge for accuracy, Lasso for diversity) in optimization to balance accuracy and diversity objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate regularizers to enforce diversification constraints during training/optimization; balance strength to avoid degrading personalization excessively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept/data drift monitoring and retraining
rubrics_metrics.description: Models (e.g., clickbait classifiers) suffer from data and concept drift as tactics change over time, requiring periodic retraining and incorporation of new semantics/patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement monitoring pipelines for drift detection, schedule retraining or online updating, and include mechanisms to incorporate newly emerging linguistic/syntactic patterns.
